summary: Specifies how LDP can be extended to set up constraint-based routed label-switched paths, using new TLVs. This lets an operator choose paths by requirements such as bandwidth instead of only the shortest route. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Normal directions give you the shortest road. This lets a network pick a road that also meets rules, like having enough room for a big truck.

questions: how to set up constrained lsps
how does cr-ldp set up an lsp
what is an explicit route in mpls
subtitle: Extends LDP so an MPLS network can set up label-switched paths that follow explicit routes and meet resource constraints.

tldr.problem: Paths set up from routing tables alone cannot reserve bandwidth, follow an operator-chosen route, or avoid certain links. Operators wanted paths calculated at the network edge using more than routing information.
tldr.mechanism: CR-LDP adds new TLVs to the LDP Label Request message: an explicit route, traffic parameters, preemption priorities, a path identifier, a resource class and route pinning. The request travels hop by hop to the egress, and a Label Mapping message comes back along the same path.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 7358. It supports only unidirectional point-to-point paths.

today: RFC 3212 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 7358, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Constrain a Path
sections.content:
LDP distributes labels inside one MPLS domain. One of the most valuable services MPLS can offer is constraint-based routing: setting up a path using more than the routing protocol knows, such as explicit route constraints or QoS constraints. It is a way to meet the traffic engineering requirements of RFC 2702, and the RFC notes that MPLS-based VPNs are another use.

A CR-LSP (constraint-based routed label switched path) is still a path through an MPLS network. The difference is that it is calculated at one point at the edge of the network, based on criteria that go beyond routing information. The reasons for doing this include giving the LSP a certain bandwidth or service class, or making sure alternative routes use physically separate paths.

The document proposes an end-to-end setup mechanism initiated by the ingress LSR, plus ways to reserve resources with LDP. It covers strict and loose explicit routing, traffic parameters, route pinning, preemption through setup and holding priorities, failure handling, an LSP identifier and resource class.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular directions only say "take the shortest way". This lets the starting point plan the whole trip in advance, including which roads to use and how much room to save on them.

sections.title: The Constraints
sections.content:
An explicit route is a list of nodes or groups of nodes. Each group is called an abstract node, and the path must include all of them in order. A group lets the route generator work with imperfect knowledge of the details. A hop can be strict or loose: a loose hop may be reached through other nodes that are not part of it.

Traffic characteristics are described by a peak rate, a committed rate and a service granularity. The rates express bandwidth constraints, and the granularity can limit the delay variation the domain may introduce.

Preemption lets a new path displace existing ones if no route with enough resources exists. A new path's setup priority is compared with the holding priority of existing paths. Both run from 0 (most important) to 7 (least important), and the recommended default is 4. A setup priority should not be higher than the holding priority, or a path might bump an LSP and then be bumped by an equivalent request.

Route pinning applies to loosely routed segments and prevents the path from changing even when a better next hop appears. A resource class (also called a color or administrative group) says which classes of links the path may use.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say which towns the trip must pass through, how much space to keep, how important your trip is compared with others, and which roads are off limits. You can also say "stick to this road even if a better one opens up".

sections.title: Messages and the New TLVs
sections.content:
CR-LDP reuses the LDP messages from RFC 3036 and adds optional TLVs to them. It depends on discovery, Label Request and Label Mapping in downstream on demand mode with ordered control, Notification, Withdraw and Release messages, and loop detection for loosely routed segments. If a Label Request carries any CR-TLV, the LSR implicitly uses ordered control for that path.

The Label Request message MUST include a single FEC TLV (the CR-LSP FEC element SHOULD be used) and MUST carry the LSPID TLV. It MAY carry the explicit route, traffic, pinning, resource class and preemption TLVs. The Label Mapping message MUST include a single Label TLV and may echo the LSPID and traffic TLVs. Failures are advisory and are reported by Notification messages that carry new status codes with the F bit set.

The new TLV types live in a range of the LDP TLV space, 0x0800 to 0x08FF, which is allocated through IETF Consensus. The RFC defines TLVs for the explicit route (0x0800), four kinds of ER-Hop, traffic parameters, preemption, LSPID, resource class and route pinning. A new FEC element type, CR-LSP (0x04), has no value octets.

The LSPID TLV identifies a CR-LSP uniquely by the ingress LSR router ID (or any of its IPv4 addresses) together with a locally unique CR-LSP ID. It also carries a 4-bit action flag: 0000 for initial setup and 0001 for modify. The procedure for modify is defined in RFC 3214.
sections.plainLanguage: CR-LDP does not invent a new language. It adds extra labeled boxes to the messages LDP already sends, and each box holds one kind of rule.

sections.title: Explicit Routes and ER-Hops
sections.content:
The ER-TLV holds one or more ER-Hop TLVs. Each has an L bit: set means loose, cleared means strict. Four hop types are defined: an IPv4 prefix (0x0801, prefix length 1 to 32, where 32 names a single node), an IPv6 prefix (0x0802, length 1 to 128), an autonomous system number (0x0803) and an LSPID (0x0804). A node that gets an unsupported ER-Hop type MUST NOT forward the request and MUST send back a "No Route" notification.

The LSPID hop lets one CR-LSP be stacked inside another, or spliced onto an existing one, which helps local repair. Tunnelled segments need an LDP session between the tunnel end points.

At each node the next hop is chosen in steps. The node checks the first ER-Hop: if it is strict and the node is not part of it, that is a "Bad Initial ER-Hop Error". If there is no second hop, the ER-TLV is removed. If the node is also part of the second hop, the first hop is deleted and the check repeats. If the node is adjacent to the second hop's abstract node, it picks a next hop there. Otherwise it picks a next hop toward it, with errors for a strict hop with no path ("Bad Strict Node Error") or a loose hop with no path inside the domain ("Bad Loose Node Error"). Finally the node replaces the first hop so the next node will accept the route. Which path to choose is implementation dependent, and nodes are assumed to make a best effort to find a loop-free path.

After selecting a next hop, a node may add ER-Hops. A node inside the first hop's abstract node may insert hops that denote subsets of it, and if the first hop is loose, an arbitrary series may be inserted before it.
sections.plainLanguage: The route is a list of stops, and each stop can be an exact place or a whole neighborhood. Each stop is crossed off as you go, until you reach the last one.

sections.title: Traffic Parameters and Preemption
sections.content:
The Traffic Parameters TLV (0x0810, length 24) carries a Flags field, a Frequency, a Weight and five values: peak data rate (PDR), peak burst size (PBS), committed data rate (CDR), committed burst size (CBS) and excess burst size (EBS). Each is a 32-bit IEEE single-precision number, with rates in bytes per second and sizes in bytes. PDR MUST be greater than or equal to CDR.

The peak rate is a token-bucket style limit defined by PDR and PBS. The committed rate uses a bucket sized CBS and a second bucket sized EBS, which measures how far traffic exceeds the commitment. Edge actions such as passing, marking or dropping are specific to the MPLS domain. Frequency says how finely the committed rate is made available: Unspecified (0), Frequent (1) or VeryFrequent (2). Weight, from 1 to 255, sets the path's relative share of excess bandwidth, and 0 means not applicable.

Each parameter has a negotiable flag. If it is set, an LSR MAY replace the value with a smaller one. After negotiation, an LSR that can support the parameters MUST reserve the resources, and otherwise MUST send a Notification with "Resource Unavailable". The egress must return the negotiated values in the Label Mapping message, and other LSRs SHOULD adjust their reservations if they differ.

The Preemption TLV (0x0820) holds a setup priority and a holding priority. Paths set up without it SHOULD be treated as having the default priorities, for example 4. When an established LSP is preempted, the preempting LSR sends a Withdraw upstream and a Release downstream. For a path still being set up, it sends a Notification upstream and an Abort downstream.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the network the most traffic you will send at once and the amount you want guaranteed. If the road cannot give you that much, it may offer less, and everyone along the way adjusts.

sections.title: Status Codes and Failures
sections.content:
CR-LDP gives the LDP status code space a new range, 0x04000000 to 0x040000FF, for errors in establishing a CR-LSP and in processing CR-TLVs. All of the new status codes require the F bit to be set. Notifications MUST be forwarded toward the LSR that originated the Label Request.

Some failures have specific rules. If an LSR receives a Traffic Parameters TLV where PDR is less than CDR in a Label Request, it MUST send a Notification with "Traffic Parameters Unavailable" upstream. In a Label Mapping message, it MUST send a Label Release with that status, and should also send a Notification upstream with "Label Request Aborted". An LSR that receives a Notification for a CR-LSP SHOULD release any resources it reserved for it.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the network sends a message back with a number that says what, and everyone releases the space they were holding.

sections.title: Setup Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through a strict route over four LSRs (LSR1 to LSR4). LSR1 sends a Label Request whose ER-TLV holds three IPv4 hops with prefix length 32, one per node: <a, b, c>. Each node removes its own hop before passing the request on, so LSR2 forwards <b, c> and LSR3 forwards <c>. At LSR4 no second hop exists, so the ER-TLV is removed and LSR4, as egress, sends a Label Mapping message back. LSR3 and LSR2 each pass it upstream until LSR1 receives it and the end-to-end CR-LSP is set up.

A second example mixes groups of nodes and specific nodes. Nodes inside a group forward the request to another member of the group, still following normal routing toward the specific node, until a node is adjacent to that specific node.

Appendix B shows how traffic parameters build services. A delay-sensitive service sets CDR and CBS equal to PDR and PBS and asks for Frequent service. A throughput-sensitive service sets all four values and signals Unspecified frequency. In both cases, edge actions are agreed in a service level agreement and are not signaled.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stop on the list reads its own line, crosses it off, and hands the rest of the list to the next stop. At the end, a reply goes back the same way to say the road is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: CR-LDP adds no security mechanism of its own. It inherits the one in Section 4.0 of RFC 3036, which protects against the introduction of spoofed TCP segments into LDP session connection streams.
sections.plainLanguage: CR-LDP uses the same lock that normal LDP already uses on its connections, and does not add a new one.

items.desc: The explicit route TLV has no first ER-Hop.

items.label: Bad Strict Node Error
items.desc: No path to a strict hop.

items.label: Bad Loose Node Error
items.desc: No path inside the MPLS domain to a loose hop.

items.label: Bad Initial ER-Hop Error
items.desc: Strict first hop that does not include the receiving node.

items.label: Traffic Parameters Unavailable
items.desc: For example, PDR is less than CDR.

items.label: LSP Preempted
items.desc: Path was displaced by a higher-priority path.

items.desc: A modify request cannot be handled.

items.label: Explicit Route TLV
items.desc: List of ER-Hops describing the path.

items.desc: A node or set of nodes by IPv4 prefix.

items.desc: A node or set of nodes by IPv6 prefix.

items.desc: All nodes in an autonomous system.

items.desc: An existing CR-LSP, for stacking or splicing.
